audits.mathematicalReason: The corresponding straight portions have equal lengths and cancel. The two semicircular ends together contribute one full circumference, and the outside radius exceeds the inside radius by 6 m. Thus the extra lap distance is 2π(6) = 12π m. At the same constant speed v, the extra distance equals v times the extra time, so 36v = 12π and v = π/3 m/s. Both mapped quantitative procedures are directly used.

figureEvidence.fact: The inner and outer boundaries have aligned straight-to-semicircle junctions, so their corresponding straight portions have equal lengths.
The marked perpendicular separation between the boundaries is 6 m; in the constant-width track configuration, the corresponding semicircle radii differ by 6 m.

audits.mathematicalReason: Set BH = x and AH = h. Since CH = 8 − x, the two right triangles give h² + x² = 49 and h² + (8 − x)² = 81. Subtraction yields x = 2, hence CH = 6 and h = 3√5. Because H lies on BC, BQ bisects angle ABH and CP bisects angle ACH. The angle-bisector theorem gives AQ/QH = 7/2 and AP/PH = 9/6. Therefore QH = 2h/9 and PH = 2h/5. Consequently PQ = PH − QH = (8/45)h = (8/15)√5. The proposed Pythagorean and angle-bisector scopes accurately describe this method.

figureEvidence.fact: H lies on side BC, and the altitude AH intersects CE at P and BD at Q.
The displayed order along the altitude is A, P, Q, H, consistent with using PQ = PH − QH.

routes.label: Find the top area by similarity
Locate the perpendicular cut in coordinates

audits.mathematicalReason: Place the top square at [0,2] × [0,2], with M = (0,1), upper-right vertex U = (2,2), and lower-right vertex V = (2,0). The first cut has equation y = x/2 + 1. Its perpendicular through V is y = −2x + 4, so their intersection is F = (6/5, 8/5). Triangle B has base UV = 2 and perpendicular height 2 − 6/5 = 4/5, giving top area 4/5. Alternatively, the upper-left right triangle has legs 1 and 2 and hypotenuse √5; triangle B is similar to it with hypotenuse 2, giving the same area. The vertical prism volume is c = 2(4/5) = 8/5. Only its top and original exterior right face are iced, so s = 4/5 + 2·2 = 24/5. Thus c+s = 32/5. The surface-area scope is defensible for selecting and summing the iced faces rather than computing total prism surface area. The two geometric routes are valid alternatives.

figureEvidence.fact: The first cut joins midpoint M of the left edge to the upper-right vertex.
The right-angle marker shows that the second cut, drawn from the lower-right vertex, is perpendicular to the first cut.
Region B is the triangle adjoining the entire right edge; its other two edges are interior cuts, so they create no originally iced side faces.

audits.mathematicalReason: The equal straight portions cancel in the difference between lap lengths. Each pair of semicircular ends forms a full circle, with outside radius 6 m larger than inside radius. The extra distance is therefore 2π(6) = 12π m. Since Keiko uses the same constant speed for either lap, 36v = 12π, yielding v = π/3 m/s. The circumference-application and distance–speed–time scopes are both appropriate.

figureEvidence.fact: The inner and outer straight sections span the same aligned semicircle junctions.
The marked track width is 6 m, giving a 6 m difference between the corresponding semicircle radii.

audits.mathematicalReason: The equal sides and right angles of the inner square make the four corner right triangles congruent: their hypotenuses are equal inner-square sides, and their corresponding acute angles agree. Each therefore has legs a and b, possibly interchanged. Their total area is 4(ab/2) = 2ab, which also equals 5 − 4 = 1. Hence ab = 1/2. Alternatively, the outer side gives (a+b)² = 5, while a corner triangle gives a²+b² = 4 by Pythagoras; subtracting gives 2ab = 1. Both listed routes are valid alternatives, and the square-properties scope supports the common geometric step.

figureEvidence.fact: The left outer side is divided by an inner-square vertex into the labeled segments a and b.
There is one inner-square vertex on each outer side, leaving four corner right triangles between the squares.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let each small square have side x > 0. Four such squares form the full top row, so the large square has side 4x. The remaining rectangle has horizontal length 4x and vertical width 4x − x = 3x. Its length-to-width ratio is therefore 4x/(3x) = 4/3. Equal square sides, equal opposite rectangle sides, and the meaning of a ratio are exactly the proposed scopes.

figureEvidence.fact: The four identical squares occupy a single row across the entire top side of the large square.
The remaining rectangle spans the full width below that one-small-square-high row.

audits.mathematicalReason: Under the standard fair, independent-spinner interpretation, the three equal sectors on each spinner give nine equally likely ordered outcomes. With rows 1, 3, 5 and columns 2, 4, 6, the sum table is [3,5,7; 5,7,9; 7,9,11]. Every entry except the two 9s is prime. Thus seven of the nine outcomes are favorable, giving probability 7/9. The table-based probability and prime-number scopes are both defensible for this method.

figureEvidence.fact: The left spinner has three equal sectors labeled 1, 3, and 5.
The right spinner has three equal sectors labeled 2, 4, and 6.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let T be the midpoint of AB and the common tangency point of circles A and B. Since their radii are 1, AT = BT = 1. Circle C is tangent to AB at T, so CT = 1 and CT is perpendicular to AB. For each overlap with C, the two circle-intersection points and the two centers form a unit square; consequently each lens consists of two 90° sectors minus that square. Each lens has area 2(π/4) − 1 = π/2 − 1. The two lenses have no positive-area overlap because circles A and B are externally tangent. The requested area is π − 2(π/2 − 1) = 2. Sector area is central, with the listed tangent, square-area, and circle-area procedures supporting it. The target excludes both lenses even though the diagram shades the entire C disk.

figureEvidence.fact: The lower circles centered at A and B are externally tangent at the midpoint T of AB.
The circle centered at C lies above AB, touches AB at T, and overlaps each lower circle in a lens.
The shading covers all of circle C, including the two overlap lenses; the stem, rather than the shading alone, specifies the area to count.
